To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) The HDL cholesterol levels in the population of 20- to 29-year-olds in the United States have decreased from 1.5 mmol/L to 1.4 mmol/L between 1988-1994 and 1999-2002; 2) This decrease is associated with a 10% decrease in the number of young adults who have HDL cholesterol levels of 1.5-2.2 mmol/L; and 3)
the HDL levels are inversely predictive of the time of the first major cardiovascular event in the patients with known CAVD, including those with the treated LDL levels below the 1.8mmol/L.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel therapies that will improve HDL function.
the study of lipids and lipid-related disorders in the cardiovascular system.

understanding the role of HDL and its subfractions in cardiovascular disease and with developing new strategies to raise HDL and its anti-inflammatory properties in patients at high cardiovascular risk.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a need for more research on HDL and cardiovascular risk.
there are no clear data that support the routine use of niacin or fibrates in patients with CVD or those at high risk for cardiovascular disease.
the evidence for a causal role of HDL-C in CVD risk is not yet sufficient to support the use of HDL-C raising therapies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a new approach to the study of the effects of lipid metabolism on the lipid metabolism.

we have demonstrated that a single dose of 10 mg of rosuvastatin can significantly increase plasma HDL-cholesterol levels in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, but the effect on other lipid parameters is modest.
we have shown that the HDL of diabetic subjects is dysfunctional in its ability to protect against atherosclerosis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HDL is an important player in the pathogenesis of CVD, and that the current focus on LDL levels alone is not sufficient to fully address cardiovascular risk.
the HDL cholesterol concentration is a poor predictor of CVD risk, and that the HDL particle number is a much better predictor.
the current guidelines are not sufficient to protect the health of Canadians and the health care system.
